slide_title: Why Technical Performance Alone Is Not Enough
raw_extracted_text: Why Technical Performance Alone Is Not Enough | Evaluating quantum technologies for social implementation requires attention to technical capability, application conditions, and social decision context. | Traditional View: Linear Progress | A | B | Technical progress is often represented as a simple transition from A to B. | Reframing | the perspective | Emerging Perspective: Diffusive Growth | A | First-order | Second-order | Surrounding | Technical Capability | What can the technology execute? | Application Conditions | What must be represented and satisfied? | Social Decision Context | Under what conditions should the application proceed?

slide_title: Why Transportation Is the Initial Application Domain
raw_extracted_text: Why Transportation Is the Initial Application Domain | Transportation was selected because computational problems and operational requirements can be defined at multiple levels of realism. | Near-Term Analytical Value | • Problem instances can be explicitly defined | • Operational constraints can be enumerated and tested | • Classical baselines and public data are available | • Application-technology gaps can be examined concretely | Broader Technology Interactions | • Batteries and charging systems | • Materials discovery for transport technologies | • Vehicle technologies and operating conditions | • Transport infrastructure and service requirements | Transportation provides a concrete domain for connecting application requirements with quantum-resource interpretation.

slide_title: Research Question and Scope
raw_extracted_text: Research Question and Scope | How should transport-specific problem-instance scale and operational requirements be defined so that reported quantum-resource requirements can be meaningfully interpreted? | Current Scope | • Define transport-specific problem instances and operational constraints | • Review formulations, encodings, circuit widths, and evaluation modalities | • Compare application requirements with current quantum-routing evidence | • Conduct an exploratory EVRP-side analysis to identify modeling requirements | Next-Step Question | How do these application requirements translate into formulation-specific quantum-resource requirements? | This separation keeps the present WIP focused on defining application requirements before claiming a resource estimate or quantum utility.

slide_title: Core Logic of the Study
raw_extracted_text: Core Logic of the Study | Quantum-resource estimates become meaningful only after the application requirements and their mathematical representation have been defined. | Application Requirements | Problem-instance scale | Operational constraints | Required outputs | Mathematical Representation | Decision variables | Constraint terms | Auxiliary variables | Quantum Formulation and Encoding | Problem-to-circuit mapping | Encoding choices | Compilation assumptions | Quantum-Resource Requirements | Circuit width | Circuit depth | Gate count / connectivity | Feasible Technology Stage | Simulation | Hardware execution | Resource estimation | Application requirements determine what must be represented; what must be represented determines formulation, encoding, and resource requirements.

slide_title: Literature Review: What Was Examined
raw_extracted_text: Literature Review: What Was Examined | This study adapts application-oriented benchmarking concepts to a literature-based comparison rather than executing a standardized benchmark suite. | Reviewed Evidence in This Study | • Transport problem class | • Reported problem-instance scale | • Mathematical formulation | • Quantum encoding | • Reported circuit width | • Evaluation modality | • Alignment with transport application requirements | Application-Oriented Benchmarking Perspective | • Feasible problem size | • Application-derived circuit | • Circuit width and depth | • Solution quality | • Execution time and resource use | Adaptation: use reported evidence from quantum-routing studies to compare how application requirements are represented, rather than running a new standardized benchmark suite.

slide_title: Key Finding 2: Three Types of Application-Technology Gap
raw_extracted_text: Key Finding 2: Three Types of Application-Technology Gap | The gap between current quantum-routing studies and social implementation is not only a scale gap, but also a representation gap and an evidence gap. | Scale Gap | • Customers | • Vehicles | • Depots | • Geographic scope | Representation Gap | • Payload | • Operating time | • Range | • S | tate of Charge | • Charging | • Fleet heterogeneity | Evidence Gap | • Formulation only | • Classical simulation | • Quantum simulation | • Hardware execution | • Resource estimation | Implication: quantum-resource comparisons should report not only problem scale, but also which requirements are represented and how the result was validated or estimated.

slide_title: Application-Side Definition
raw_extracted_text: Application-Side Definition | A larger instance is not necessarily more representative; application relevance depends on both problem-instance scale and operational-constraint coverage. | Problem-Instance Scale | • Customers or delivery locations | • Vehicles and depots | • Route candidates | • Geographic coverage | Operational-Constraint Coverage | • Payload | • Operating and service time | • Travel distance and range | • Time windows | • S | tate of Charge | • Charging access and duration | • Fleet heterogeneity | Problem-Instance Scale | Operational- | Constraint | Coverage | Toy | Instance | Small Instance | Rich Constraints | Large Instance | Basic Constraints | Operationally | Representative | Requirements | Application-side definition = Problem-instance scale × Required operational constraints. This definition is the basis for interpreting formulations, circuit widths, and resource estimates.

slide_title: What the Constraint Results Imply for Modeling
raw_extracted_text: What the Constraint Results Imply for Modeling | The analysis identifies which application conditions may need to be represented before formulation and resource estimation. | Constraint | Provisional Result | Modeling Implication | Payload | 0.0% unmet | Capacity was not binding under current demand assumptions | Operating time | 33.5% unmet | Time and service duration should be represented | Range | 64.4% unmet | EV range cannot be omitted from the model | SOC | Not evaluated | Sequential SOC modeling is required | Charging access | 10.7% unmet | Geographic access alone is insufficient | Charging-assisted range | 33.3% unmet | Charging support changes feasibility | Charging duration | 15.3% unmet | Charger power and duration conditions matter | Interpretation: model-conditional unmet rates are not observed failures; they are signals for deciding which constraints require explicit representation.

slide_title: Variation Across Scenarios and One-at-a-Time Parameter Changes
raw_extracted_text: Variation Across Scenarios and One-at-a-Time Parameter Changes | Quantum-resource estimates may depend strongly on application assumptions such as fleet size, usable range, service time, and route-distance representation. | High Response to Parameter Changes | • Operating-time limit | • Range feasibility | • Charging-assisted range | • Charging-duration feasibility | Lower Response Under Current Assumptions | • Payload capacity | • Charging-station access | Not Yet Assessable | • SOC feasibility requires sequential state-of-charge modeling | Main implication: before comparing qubit counts or resource estimates, assumptions about vehicle count, usable range, service time, and route-distance representation must be made explicit and comparable.

slide_title: Comparison with Current Quantum-VRP Evidence
raw_extracted_text: Comparison with Current Quantum-VRP Evidence | Current quantum-VRP studies do not yet provide a consistent basis for application evaluation because scale, operational representation, and validation evidence are not aligned across studies. | Scale Coverage | Customer, vehicle, and route-candidate scales vary considerably across studies. | Comparable scale indicators are needed. | Constraint Representation | Core routing constraints are partially represented; EV-specific constraints remain limited. | Requirement representation should be separated from validation. | Validation Evidence | Evaluation modalities differ across formulation, simulation, hardware execution, and resource estimation. | Evidence type and comparison basis must be reported. | Representation of a requirement does not necessarily mean that it has been validated under operationally representative conditions.

slide_title: Research Contribution and Next Stage
raw_extracted_text: Research Contribution and Next Stage | Contribution: This study shifts the question from “How many qubits does a published instance require?” to “What application requirements must first be represented for that qubit estimate to be meaningful?” | Direction A: Increase Operational Realism | • Road-network distances | • Observed or calibrated demand | • Time windows, SOC, and charging dynamics | • Classical optimization baseline | • Operational validation | Direction B: Develop the Application-Stage Framework | • Problem instances and required constraints | • Formulation-specific resource implications | • Expected quantum-technology stages | • Staged quantum utility | • Adjacent transport technologies and expert expectations | Operational grounding informs the application-stage framework. | How should these two directions be connected in the next research stage?
